Flatten the output of a process into rows

Source: R/flattenOutput.R
flattenOutput.Rd

The output of a process record can be anything a function returns: a single number, a named vector of indices, a data frame of detected events, a list of all of these, or nothing. flattenOutput() turns any of them into a data frame, so that the results of a process applied to many recordings, or to many windows of one, can be bound into one table.

Usage

flattenOutput(x)

Arguments

x

The output of a process, as held in the output of a record in the processing slot of a TaggedWave, or any other result.

Value

A data frame, with one row unless x is NULL or a data frame.

Details

Every column name begins with value. A table of results needs columns of its own beside these, to say which recording, which window and which process a row came from, and those can be given any name that does not begin with value without risk of clashing with a result.

The rule is:

NULL

No rows. There was nothing to flatten.

A data frame

Its rows, as they are: a detector that found five events gives five rows, and one that found none gives none. Each column is kept as it is, its name following value., so a column start is value.start. Row names the data frame was given, rather than the numbers it has by default, are kept in a column of their own, value.rownames.

Anything else

One row, as below.

Within that one row:

A single value

One column, value.

A named vector

One column for each element, its name following value.: c(mean=440, sd=7.5) gives value.mean and value.sd.

A vector without names

One column, value, holding the whole vector in a list cell.

A named list

Each element by these same rules, the names of an element and of what it holds joined by a full stop: list(n=2, b=c(x=2, y=3)) gives value.n, value.b.x and value.b.y. An element that is NULL gives no column.

A data frame within a list

One column for each of its columns, holding the value where it has one row and the whole column in a list cell otherwise.

Anything else

One column, value, holding it in a list cell. This takes in a matrix, an S4 object, a list with a class of its own such as a test result, and a list or vector some of whose names are missing or repeated, whose elements could not each be given a column of their own.

A name the rule would give twice, as list(a.b=1, a=list(b=2)) would, is made unique with make.unique().

Which columns there are depends on the names in the output and never on how long its parts are, so that the rows from different recordings line up. What a column holds can depend on length, though: an unnamed vector of one value and one of five both give value, the first as a plain value and the second in a list cell, and a data frame within a list gives plain values for one row and list cells for more. A detector that finds one peak in one window and three in the next therefore gives the same column of two types, and a table binding such rows needs to hold that column as a list wherever any row has a list cell in it. A column can also be missing from some rows, as where an element is NULL in one output and not in another.

The processing attribute tagApply() puts on a result that is not a wave is dropped, as it is the history of the wave rather than part of the result.

See also

tagApply(), which makes the records.

Examples

flattenOutput(0.42)
#>   value
#> 1  0.42
flattenOutput(c(mean = 440, sd = 7.5))
#>   value.mean value.sd
#> 1        440      7.5
flattenOutput(list(n = 2, peaks = c(440, 880)))
#>   value.n value.peaks
#> 1       2    440, 880
flattenOutput(data.frame(start = c(0.1, 0.6), end = c(0.3, 0.9)))
#>   value.start value.end
#> 1         0.1       0.3
#> 2         0.6       0.9
